name: Mullet

lead: The mullet is a hairstyle cut shorter at the front, top and sides and longer at the back. In recent years it has returned as a men's style, often combined with fades and tapers for a cleaner outline than the 1980s version.

It is a style choice rather than a treatment: the cut changes the shape of the head and face by adding length at the back and texture on top. No studies have assessed its effect on attractiveness; it is documented here through fashion history and forum discussion.

paras: People get a mullet from a barber, often asking for a taper fade on the sides with longer, textured hair at the back. Forum members ask whether it works with straight hair and describe styling hair by hand for texture. Growing the back to length takes months.
There are no medical risks. The main downsides are social and aesthetic: forum members disagree about how the cut is perceived, and it can require months of growing and regular upkeep.

angle.text: The mullet changes the shape and texture of the hair around the head. People choose it for a trend-led, high-contrast style, and modern versions pair it with fades or tapers.

lead: The mullet is a hairstyle cut shorter at the front, top and sides and left longer at the back.[1] People who wear it use the length at the back and the contrast with the sides to create a distinctive silhouette, add texture and change the outline of the head and neck.

Wikipedia reports that the Beastie Boys popularised the word with their 1994 song 'Mullet Head' and a 1995 magazine article; an apparent 1992 citation that suggested earlier use was later found to be fake. Similar cuts appear much earlier in history, from reports about the Roman emperor Tiberius to a 'Hunnic' style linked to the Byzantine Blue faction.[1]

The cut has had several waves: Tom Jones wore one in 1965, David Bowie and Paul McCartney in the 1970s, it was widely worn in the 1980s, and it revived in the 2020s, with i-D calling 2020 'the year of the mullet' and pairing with fades and tapers giving it a cleaner modern outline.[1] No published studies have examined how the cut affects perceived attractiveness; the cut is documented here through fashion history and forum discussion.[2][3]
infobox: Short front, top and sides; long back

paras: The defining feature is the contrast in length: short hair at the front, top and sides and longer hair at the back, kept off the eyes while covering the neck.[1] Researcher Alan Henderson, cited by Wikipedia, notes that this arrangement keeps hair out of the eyes while protecting the neck.[1]

Wikipedia lists variations such as the rattail, a single long, sometimes braided strand left at the back of the neck, and the skullet, in which the top and sides are shaved with hair left long at the back; the comedian Bill Bailey is named as its best-known wearer.[1] Modern versions often blend a longer back with fades or tapers on the sides, which forum members call a taper mullet.[1][2]

Wikipedia reports that Tiberius was said to wear his hair long at the back, that a bust of Caligula shows a similar cut, and that ancient texts connect the style with Hector of Troy and with the Byzantine Blue faction, where it was called the 'Hunnic' look. A first-century figurine may suggest ancient Britons wore similar cuts.[1]

The article also notes that Samoset, an Abenaki man, was described in 1621 with long hair at the back, and that several Borneo groups, including the Penan, Kayan, Kenyah and Iban, have worn mullet-style hair.[1]

Tom Jones wore a mullet during his 1965 Ed Sullivan Show appearances, and David Bowie and Paul McCartney wore versions in the 1970s, a style related to the shag.[1] In the 1980s the cut was widely popular in Australia, the US, the UK and continental Europe; Kiefer Sutherland has said his look in The Lost Boys (1987) helped spark the trend.[1] In some communities it also became a marker of lesbian identity.[1]

In 1993 Superman was drawn with a mullet in a comic storyline, and punk and alternative acts including the Vandals and Wesley Willis wrote songs about the style. The 2001 documentary American Mullet explored the trend, and in the 2000s the cut became associated with bogan subculture in Australia and New Zealand.[1]
Iran banned the mullet in 2010 as a 'decadent Western' style. Athletes and coaches including Patrick Kane, Mike Gundy and James Conner helped revive it in sport.[1]

i-D called 2020 'the year of the mullet', crediting lockdowns and salon closures, and an annual USA Mullet Championship began that year.[1] In 2023 the singer Peso Pluma made the style his signature look, and Tami Manis earned a Guinness record for her long mullet.[1] Wikipedia describes the modern version as often combining the long back with a fade or taper and calls it a major men's hair trend of 2026.[1]

On looksmax.org, one thread asks whether a mullet is 'viable' with straight hair and which version has more appeal; one reply says it would look poor with straight hair, and the original poster answers that his hair is not very straight and holds texture when styled by hand.[2]

Another thread asks for views on the modern mullet and includes the claim that it is a good style if the wearer is neurotypical with a friend group, but is seen negatively otherwise. A reply asks whether it has appeal on dating apps, and a further reply says it does and suggests pairing it with good clothes.[3] These posts show divided opinion on how the cut is perceived.

People get a mullet from a barber, often asking for a taper fade on the sides with longer, textured hair at the back, and forum members describe styling by hand for texture.[2] Growing the back to length takes months.

lore.intro: Looksmax.org members discuss the mullet as a style option, with debate about hair type and social perception.[2][3]
